constraint_review: Load about 60 kg: met, design carries 60 kg parcel as part of 67.1 kg total lift and 658 N weight with 118 N m parcel moment checked. Operated by one person: met, tare lift 69.7 N with tip-back pull 118 N and brake release 57.4 N are all one-hand loads and slope is held hands-off by lock.
feedback:
The tri-star dead-man truck works physically and I would release it to detail design. The parcel sits on a toe-plate and straps to a twin-tube backbone that bends to a main axle carried by two tri-star clusters that pivot over the 197 mm riser, while a spring-applied disc plus tooth pin holds the slope when the handle is released. My main worry is no longer principle but refinement: cable slack management for the sliding handle and the feel of tooth re-engagement under load, plus tidying the van-door proof. Against the closest prior art, the combination of patent US4142732A plus fixed-frame 60 kg skid truck, this is a real step: Boyd is squeeze-to-brake band friction only that free-wheels if let go, and the skid truck is fully welded fixed frame with no brake, whereas v4 is release-to-lock dead-man with positive tooth engagement and folding twin-tube backbone for diagonal van stow.

Re-check of the four items from the last loop. Backbone deflection with correct cantilever model is now met. The board abandoned the idea that the clip-on transverse brace grounds the cantilever tip and now treats deflection as delta equals F times L cubed over 3 times E times I-total with 1.1 m length and twin-tube inertia (E116), giving tip whip 43.9 mm for 589 N parcel load, and bending stress sigma equals M times c over I per tube with 1.5 impact giving 40.9 MPa at the unified 118 N m moment (E118) (E90). That directly answers the ask and the numbers recompute. Folded envelope with full stack is now met in substance. The board replaced the impossible 730 mm claim with a stacked length 1145 mm from 1100 mm backbone plus 35 mm overhang plus 10 mm cap (E104), stacked width 380 mm from 310 mm axle plus two times 35 mm cluster thickness (E105), and stacked thickness 190 mm from 185 mm cluster radius plus 5 mm clearance (E106), shown in side-view deployed versus folded sketch with brace alongside (E108) and checked against 1120 mm door width with minus 25 mm straight clearance (E107) so entry uses a 1.67 m diagonal (E109) to a 1.80 m floor from small-van data (E36). Stair work and holding torque from one total mass are now met and reconciled. Total lift energy per riser 129 J from mass times g times height with 66.7 kg total (E96) matches my recompute 128.9 J, slope load 403 N from total weight 658 N times sin theta 0.613 (E123) (E122), total lock torque 74.6 N m from slope load times 0.185 m cluster radius (E124), and per-side torque 37.3 N m as half the total (E132), so the old 67.0 N m total versus 38.8 to 39.0 N m per-side split is superseded. Hand force and pin shear calculation is present andMath-correct but sourcing remains weak. Clamp 1.55 kN from total torque over 0.0479 m effective friction radius (E100) resting on pad-force times friction times rotor radius physics taken from opened bicycle-brake analysis (E111), hand release 57.4 N from clamp over lever ratio 8 and 4.5 and 0.75 cable efficiency (E101), and pin shear ratio 0.498 (E102) all recompute to 57.4 N and 0.498, yet the Snook and ISO push-pull and grip limits cited are still search-result-only pages never opened, so the formal set-against-published-limits part is not fully evidenced; by everyday scale 57.4 N is about 5.9 kgf two-finger pull and clearly one-person feasible, so I do not hold the concept for it.

Formulas and worst case. Backbone uses linear elastic cantilever bending, valid for long slender aluminium tubes below yield, with second moment for 40 by 36 mm tubes 4.32e-08 m4 (E113) doubling for twin tubes; my check 589 N times 1.331 m3 over 3 times 68.9 GPa times 8.64e-08 m2 gives 0.0439 m, i.e. 43.9 mm, and stress 58.9 N m per tube times 0.02 m over 4.32e-08 m2 times 1.5 gives 40.9 MPa against 276 MPa yield, safety factor about 6.7, so impact and full 200 mm offset are covered. Stair model uses E equals m times g times h for quasi-static lift and T equals W times sin theta times R for holding on the 37.8 degree max slope from 197 mm riser over 254 mm going, with sin theta 0.613, which is the correct steepest domestic stair and therefore the hardest holding case; descent power about 80 W at 0.2 m per s from earlier simulation is ordinary human metering power. Brake model assumes Coulomb disc torque equals clamp times effective friction radius, valid for slow slip holding, plus a shear pin that carries the slope if friction fades; ratio 0.498 implies factor about 2 on the pin, and hands-off holding means the 403 N slope, about 41 kgf or about 0.6 body weights, never relies on sustained 188 N grip that would exceed 130 to 140 N sustained guidance. Everyday checks pass: tare 7.1 kg at 69.7 N (E131) is a suitcase lift, tip-back 118 N at 1.0 m handle (E110) is about 12 kgf, 129 J per riser is lifting shopping for one step, and 1145 mm length is a tall person lying down that cannot pass straight through a 1120 mm door but easily angles through a tall door diagonal.

The design agrees with itself. Function by function: support by folding toe-plate 365 by 240 mm, restraint by webbing strap, flat roll by paired small wheels inside each tri-star, stair walking by tri-star cluster 370 mm overall with 150 mm wheels, limiting by disc with tooth lock plus dead-man lever and cable, collapse by folding toe and sliding handle with clip-on brace alongside, all present in parts, connections, operating sequence and chief selections, so no missing function (check 0). Mass adds as 60 kg parcel plus 6.5 kg truck plus 0.2 kg brace plus 0.37 kg upsize penalty to 67.1 kg (E121), weight 658 N (E122), and envelope adds as above to 1145 by 380 by 190 mm, which does leave toe thickness, disc thickness and strap bulk implicit but all are smaller than the bounding clusters and backbone, so the sums carry the driving parts (check 1). Numeric limits are computed, not words-only: parcel weight 589 N (E7), total weight, slope, torque, release, whip and stacks all have arithmetic (check 1b). Where two values existed the design now uses the reconciled ones: total mass 67.1 kg not 66.5 kg, total torque 74.6 N m not 67.0 N m, per-side 37.3 N m not 39.0 N m, length 1145 mm not 730 mm, stress 40.9 MPa with impact for 40 mm tubes not 51.1 MPa without impact or 76.7 MPa for 30 mm tubes; residual 0.4 N m between 74.2 N m used for clamp and 74.6 N m final is 0.5 percent and immaterial, and 129 J using 66.7 kg versus 129.7 J using 67.1 kg is the same (check 2). Load flows toe-plate to backbone to axle to clusters, signal flows grip lever tension through slack loop to caliper and tooth pin to axle with fold order brake-locked so sliding never releases, and deployed versus folded states are kept distinct with one-piece backbone kept for rigidity (check 3). No blocking objection remains open and all four members marked ready, so there is nothing unsettled to overrule (check 4). The 1235 mm side used in the 1.67 m diagonal is unlabeled and the door-height source should be cited explicitly in detail design, and push-pull limits should be replaced by an opened ergonomics page, but neither can fail the concept because straight length already fits the 1802 mm floor and 25 mm door interference is cleared by any small angle. Keep the bench questions on lever feel and tooth wear as detail-design tests, not concept gates.
